planMarkdown:
Bot: Production-ready Telegram Trading and Sniper Bot Plan

Summary:
Build a fast Telegram bot that lets users manage wallets, buy and sell tokens, configure snipes, track positions, and receive safety warnings before risky actions.

The bot should be designed as a single Node.js service using grammY for Telegram interactions, MongoDB for durable state, and a chain adapter layer for wallet, pricing, liquidity, and transaction execution. The product should prioritize short replies, inline buttons, clear confirmations, strong private-key handling, and safe defaults.

Product goals:
1) Give users a simple trading interface inside Telegram.

Users should be able to create, import, or connect a wallet, then trade with commands such as /buy, /sell, /snipe, /balance, and /positions. The bot should avoid long forms and instead use short prompts, inline buttons, and reusable presets.

2) Make sniping configurable but not overwhelming.

Snipe settings should include trade amount, slippage, max buy, gas or priority fee where supported, liquidity threshold, start condition, and optional auto-sell rules such as take-profit and stop-loss. Users should be able to save defaults globally and override them for a specific token.

3) Track positions clearly.

For every token position, the bot should show size, average entry price, current estimated value, realized PnL, unrealized PnL, total cost, and relevant transaction history. PnL should be presented as an estimate when pricing data is incomplete or liquidity is thin.

4) Protect users from common mistakes.

The bot should warn about low liquidity, suspicious token properties, high slippage, unusually large trades, failed simulation, excessive exposure, and transactions above the user’s configured max percentage per trade. Big buys should require explicit confirmation.

5) Keep actions fast.

Common actions should fit into one or two taps after initial setup. The bot should cache non-sensitive market data briefly, keep user settings ready in memory after loading from MongoDB, and use short status updates such as preparing, submitted, confirmed, or failed.

High-level architecture:
1) Single service structure.

Run one Node.js ESM process that owns the Telegram bot, user session handling, trading orchestration, wallet operations, MongoDB access, and in-process background tasks. The service starts grammY using TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables and initializes MongoDB plus chain adapters on boot.

2) Main modules.

Telegram interface: grammY command handlers, callback query handlers, conversations or stateful flows, error boundaries, rate limits, and compact message formatting.

User and settings service: loads and saves user profiles, wallet metadata, trading defaults, snipe presets, safety limits, and notification preferences.

Wallet service: supports wallet creation, import, and external connection metadata. For created or imported wallets, private keys must be encrypted before persistence. The bot should never display a private key after setup except through a deliberate export flow with repeated confirmation.

Trading service: validates inputs, computes trade size, checks safety rules, estimates output, builds transactions, requests confirmation when needed, submits transactions, tracks status, and updates positions.

Snipe service: maintains active snipe rules in MongoDB and an in-memory runtime registry. It polls or subscribes through supported chain data sources where available, evaluates trigger conditions, performs safety checks, and executes configured buys. Since the service is a single process, in-process scheduling is acceptable, with MongoDB used as the source of truth for recovery after restart.

Position service: reconciles buys, sells, fees, token balances, and price estimates into position records. It should update immediately after bot-initiated trades and periodically reconcile against on-chain balances.

Risk engine: evaluates max percentage per trade, liquidity, slippage, token age if available, ownership or authority flags where supported, transfer restrictions if detectable, tax or fee behavior where detectable, and whether the trade simulation looks abnormal.

Market data and chain adapter layer: abstracts the target blockchain and trading venue details. It exposes methods for balances, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction submission, and confirmation tracking.

3) Interaction model.

Commands start flows, inline buttons handle quick decisions, and callback data should be compact and signed or mapped to server-side state to avoid trusting client-provided values. Messages should be edited in place for status updates when possible to reduce chat noise.

4) Reliability model.

All critical actions should be idempotent. A trade request gets an internal action id before transaction submission. If Telegram retries an update or a user taps twice, the service should detect duplicate action ids and prevent double execution. MongoDB stores transaction state transitions so the bot can resume pending confirmations after restart.

5) Security model.

Use environment variables for secrets, encrypt sensitive wallet material, separate display data from secret data, require confirmation for exports and large trades, and redact secrets from logs. Admin-only diagnostics should be gated by Telegram user id allowlists stored in configuration or MongoDB.

Data model:
1) User.

Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, createdAt, lastSeenAt, status, defaultWalletId, riskProfile, globalTradingSettings, notificationSettings, role, and feature flags.

2) Wallet.

Fields: walletId, telegramUserId, chain, type, publicAddress, encryptedSecret if custodial or imported, connectionMetadata if externally connected, label, createdAt, lastUsedAt, archivedAt, and exportLockedUntil if needed.

3) Trading settings.

Fields: telegramUserId, defaultAmount, defaultSlippageBps, maxBuyAmount, maxPercentPerTrade, gasOrPriorityFeePreset, customFeeValue, requireConfirmationAboveAmount, autoSellDefaults, mevOrprivacyPreference if applicable to the chain, and updatedAt.

4) Snipe order.

Fields: snipeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol if known, status, amount, slippageBps, maxBuyAmount, minimumLiquidity, gasOrPriorityFee, triggerType, triggerParams, autoSellTakeProfitPercent, autoSellStopLossPercent, expiresAt, createdAt, updatedAt, executedTradeId, failureReason, and retryPolicy.

5) Trade.

Fields: tradeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, side, tokenAddress, baseAsset, requestedAmount, estimatedOutput, actualInput, actualOutput, slippageBps, feeEstimate, transactionHash, status, riskSnapshot, quoteSnapshot, confirmationRequired, confirmationStatus, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt, submittedAt, confirmedAt, and finalizedAt.

6) Position.

Fields: positionId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol, tokenDecimals, status, size, averageEntryPrice, totalCost, realizedPnl, unrealizedPnlEstimate, currentPriceEstimate, currentValueEstimate, feesPaidEstimate, openedAt, updatedAt, and closedAt.

7) Token risk snapshot.

Fields: chain, tokenAddress, checkedAt, liquidityEstimate, holderOrdistributionSignals if available, ownershipOrauthoritySignals if available, transferRestrictionSignals if available, simulationResult, warnings, severity, and dataQuality.

8) Session state.

Use grammY session storage backed by MongoDB for durable multi-step flows. Short-lived non-critical state can be held in memory, but anything related to pending trades, confirmations, wallet setup, or active snipes should be persisted.

9) Audit log.

Store user-visible security and trading events: wallet created, wallet imported, export requested, settings changed, snipe created, snipe cancelled, trade confirmed, trade submitted, trade failed, and admin action. Do not store raw secrets in audit records.

Key flows:
1) Onboarding and wallet setup.

User sends /start. The bot explains the core actions and asks the user to create, import, or connect a wallet. Create generates a wallet, stores encrypted secret material, shows the public address, and tells the user to back up through a secure export flow. Import asks for the private key or seed only inside a strict flow, validates it, encrypts it, and deletes sensitive prompt messages when possible. Connect stores external wallet metadata and explains which actions may require external approval.

2) Buy flow.

User sends /buy token amount or taps Buy from a token card. The bot resolves token metadata, loads wallet and settings, fetches a quote, runs risk checks, and replies with a compact preview: token, amount in, estimated amount out, price impact, slippage, liquidity warning if any, and fee estimate. If the trade is small and within safety limits, the user can confirm with one tap or use a saved fast-buy preset. If the trade exceeds thresholds, the bot requires explicit confirmation.

3) Sell flow.

User sends /sell token percent or chooses from /positions. The bot shows current position, estimated value, PnL, price impact, and expected output. Quick buttons should include 25%, 50%, 100%, and custom. The bot runs the same quote, simulation, and risk checks before submission.

4) Snipe setup flow.

User sends /snipe token. The bot shows a settings summary with amount, slippage, max buy, fee preset, liquidity threshold, and auto-sell. The user can create immediately with defaults or edit individual fields. Once activated, the snipe appears in active snipes and can be paused or cancelled.

5) Snipe execution flow.

The snipe service monitors active rules. When a trigger is met, it revalidates wallet balance, amount limits, liquidity, quote, token risk, and fee settings. If the rule is still valid, it creates a trade record, submits the transaction, updates the user with status, and updates the related position on confirmation. If auto-sell is enabled, it creates monitoring rules for take-profit and stop-loss after the buy is confirmed.

6) Balance and positions flow.

/balance shows wallet address, base asset balance, estimated token portfolio value, and any data quality warning. /positions lists open positions with symbol, size, entry, current estimate, and PnL. Selecting a position opens actions: sell, refresh, set auto-sell, view trades, or hide dust.

7) Safety flow.

Before any risky action, the risk engine returns a severity level: info, warning, high risk, or blocked. Info and normal warnings can be acknowledged with a tap. High-risk trades require an explicit confirmation phrase or a second confirmation step. Blocked trades should explain the reason and show settings that can be adjusted only if it is safe to allow override.

8) Recovery flow.

On startup, the service loads pending trades and active snipes from MongoDB. It checks any transaction that was submitted but not finalized, reconciles positions, and rebuilds the in-memory snipe registry. Users should not need to recreate snipes after a restart.

Tech stack:
1) Runtime and language.

Use a single Node.js service with ESM modules. The Telegram bot uses grammY and reads the bot token from TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN in environment variables.

2) Persistence.

Use MongoDB for users, wallets, settings, snipes, trades, positions, sessions, and audit logs. In-memory maps may be used only for short-lived caches, callback correlation, rate limiting, and active runtime registries that can be rebuilt from MongoDB.

3) Telegram framework.

Use grammY middleware for sessions, command routing, callback queries, conversations or structured multi-step flows, error handling, and rate limiting. Keep handlers thin and move business logic into services.

4) Blockchain integration.

Create a chain adapter interface for wallet derivation or validation, balance reads, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction building, submission, and confirmation tracking. This keeps the bot adaptable if the target chain or venue changes.

5) Storage for files.

If the bot later needs generated reports, exported CSV files, or chart images, store them in object storage or simple filesystem storage. Do not store wallet secrets in files.

6) Deployment.

Deploy as a generic Node.js server in the cloud. Use environment variables for configuration, a managed process lifecycle, health checks, structured logs, and regular MongoDB backups. No additional databases, message queues, or external infrastructure are required for the core design.

Non-functional requirements:
1) Security.

Encrypt private wallet material before storing it. Keep encryption keys outside MongoDB in environment-managed secrets. Never log private keys, seed phrases, raw signed transactions if sensitive, or full user-provided secrets. Add confirmation gates for wallet export, big trades, and dangerous settings.

2) Performance.

Most command responses should acknowledge within one second, even if execution continues asynchronously. Use short-lived caches for token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, and user settings. Edit existing Telegram messages for progress updates instead of sending many new messages.

3) Reliability.

Persist every trade before submission. Use clear transaction states: created, awaiting confirmation, submitted, confirmed, failed, expired, and reconciled. Make callback actions idempotent so repeated taps cannot execute duplicate trades.

4) Observability.

Use structured logs with request ids, telegram user ids, action ids, trade ids, and transaction hashes. Track error rates, failed quotes, failed submissions, slow chain calls, and snipe execution outcomes. Provide an admin-only status command for service health and pending operations.

5) Compliance and user communication.

Show clear risk disclaimers during onboarding and before high-risk trading. Make it obvious that PnL and price data are estimates. Provide commands to export basic user data, delete bot data where feasible, and revoke or archive wallets from the bot interface.

6) Abuse prevention.

Apply per-user rate limits, block repeated invalid token lookups, limit the number of active snipes per user by plan or configuration, and protect admin commands with an allowlist. Validate all Telegram callback data against server-side state.

7) Maintainability.

Keep Telegram handlers separate from trading logic, wallet logic, risk logic, and persistence. Use typed configuration, consistent error codes, integration tests for critical flows, and test wallets on non-production environments before enabling real trading.

Bot commands:
• start — Starts onboarding, explains the bot, and shows the main menu with wallet, trading, positions, and settings actions. (usage: /start) [core]
• wallet — Shows the active wallet, public address, wallet status, and actions to create, import, connect, export, switch, or archive a wallet. (usage: /wallet) [wallet]
• buy — Starts a token buy flow with quote preview, safety checks, and confirmation buttons. (usage: /buy <tokenaddress> <amount>) [trading]
• sell — Starts a token sell flow. Supports exact amount, percentage, or quick selection from current positions. (usage: /sell <tokenaddress> <percentoramount>) [trading]
• snipe — Creates or manages a snipe order using saved defaults, editable amount, slippage, max buy, fee, liquidity threshold, and optional auto-sell. (usage: /snipe <tokenaddress>) [sniping]
• snipes — Lists active, paused, executed, and failed snipes with actions to edit, pause, resume, or cancel. (usage: /snipes) [sniping]
• balance — Shows wallet balance, estimated portfolio value, and recent refresh status. (usage: /balance) [portfolio]
• positions — Lists open token positions with size, average entry, current estimate, and PnL. Each position opens sell, refresh, and auto-sell actions. (usage: /positions) [portfolio]
• settings — Opens trading defaults such as amount, slippage, max percent per trade, max buy, fee preset, confirmation threshold, and auto-sell defaults. (usage: /settings) [settings]
• risk — Shows or edits safety settings and can run a token risk check without trading. (usage: /risk [tokenaddress]) [safety]
• history — Shows recent trades, transaction statuses, realized PnL, and failed actions. (usage: /history) [portfolio]
• help — Shows a short command reference and recommended first steps. (usage: /help) [core]

# Trading Sniper Bot

This is a Telegram-only trading and sniping bot built with Node.js ES modules and grammY.

It helps users create or import an encrypted wallet, preview buys and sells, configure snipe targets, track positions, and edit trading safety settings.

Crypto trading and sniping are high risk. This bot is not financial advice.

## Commands

/start
Opens the main menu and shows the risk disclaimer.

/help
Shows commands, wallet requirements, safety checks, and the recommended flow.

/wallet
Create a new wallet, import a wallet, view the active public address, or delete stored wallet data.

/buy <tokenAddress> <amount> [slippage]
Starts a buy preview. The bot fetches a quote when a DEX aggregator is configured, checks risk and liquidity when configured, then requires confirmation.

/sell <tokenAddress> <amountOrPercent> [slippage]
Starts a sell preview. You can also select a position and use 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% buttons.

/snipe [tokenAddress]
Creates a guided snipe target using your defaults for amount, slippage, max buy, priority fee, take-profit, and stop-loss.

/balance
Shows native balance and tracked token positions. Requires a wallet and RPC_URL.

/positions
Shows open positions with size, average entry, and basic estimated PnL status.

/settings
Opens inline buttons to edit default amount, slippage, max buy, max percent per trade, priority fee, take-profit, stop-loss, and confirmation preferences.

## Environment variables

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required for Telegram.

MONGODB_URI enables persistent storage for users, wallets, snipes, trades, and positions. If missing, the bot starts with limited in-memory fallback.

WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET is required for wallet creation and import. Wallet secrets are encrypted at rest. Private keys and seed phrases are never logged or echoed.

RPC_URL is used for native balance checks.

CHAIN_ID defaults to 1.

NATIVE_SYMBOL defaults to ETH.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL enables quote and execution provider calls.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_API_KEY is optional and sent only to the configured aggregator.

MARKET_DATA_API_URL enables liquidity checks.

RISK_API_URL enables risky-token scoring.

TRADING_ENABLED defaults to false. When false, the bot runs quote and preview flows only.

SNIPE_POLL_INTERVAL_MS defaults to 15000.

## Safety behavior

The bot validates token addresses before trading.

It warns when quotes are unavailable, liquidity checks are unavailable, risk scoring is unavailable, liquidity appears low, the risk API reports danger, or the trade exceeds max buy settings.

All transactions require explicit confirmation. Preview mode is used when TRADING_ENABLED=false.

## MongoDB collections

users stores Telegram metadata and trading settings.

wallets stores public wallet data and encrypted secret payloads.

snipes stores active and historical snipe targets.

trades stores quote, status, transaction hash, and failure summaries.

positions stores tracked token positions and average entry data.

createdAt is insert-only. Updates use updatedAt.

## Deployment

Install dependencies with npm run build.

Start with npm start.

On Render, set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI. Add WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET before enabling wallet creation or import. Keep TRADING_ENABLED=false until provider integrations are tested.

The bot runs as one Node.js process. The snipe poller runs inside the same process.

README.md.content:
# Trading Sniper Bot

Telegram-only trading/sniping bot using Node.js ES modules, grammY, MongoDB, encrypted wallet storage, inline menus, preview-first trading, and a single-process snipe polling loop.

## Features

1) Wallet creation, import, view, and delete.
2) Encrypted wallet secrets using WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET.
3) Buy and sell preview flows with confirmation.
4) Snipe target storage and polling.
5) Balance and position views.
6) Editable trading settings.
7) Liquidity and risk warnings when APIs are configured.
8) Preview-only mode unless TRADING_ENABLED=true.

## Setup

1) Install dependencies.

npm run build

2) Copy .env.sample to .env and fill values.

3) Start locally.

npm run dev

4) Start production.

npm start

## Required env

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required.

MONGODB_URI is strongly recommended for persistence.

WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET is required before wallet creation or import works.

## Optional env

RPC_URL enables /balance.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL enables /buy and /sell quotes and execution provider calls.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_API_KEY is optional provider auth.

MARKET_DATA_API_URL enables liquidity checks.

RISK_API_URL enables token risk scoring.

TRADING_ENABLED defaults to false.

## Commands

/start opens the main menu.

/help shows usage and safety notes.

/wallet opens wallet setup.

/buy <tokenAddress> <amount> [slippage] previews a buy.

/sell <tokenAddress> <amountOrPercent> [slippage] previews a sell.

/snipe [tokenAddress] creates a snipe target.

/balance shows native balance and tracked positions.

/positions lists open positions.

/settings edits defaults and safety limits.

## Architecture

src/index.js boots the app, validates Telegram config, connects MongoDB, starts the bot, and starts the in-process snipe poller.

src/bot.js creates the grammY bot and registers command modules before catch-all flow handlers.

src/commands contains public command modules.

src/features/tradingUi.js owns inline menus, callbacks, and multi-step flows.

src/services contains wallet, user, market, trading, position, and snipe logic.

src/lib contains config, logging, database, crypto, and UI helpers.

## Database

Collections: users, wallets, snipes, trades, positions.

Indexes are created only for application fields, never _id.

Upserts keep createdAt in $setOnInsert and updatedAt in $set.

## Deployment notes

Use one Node.js service. Do not run a separate worker.

The bot clears Telegram webhooks before long polling.

The snipe poller logs start, cycles, failures, and memory usage.

Keep TRADING_ENABLED=false until your RPC, aggregator, risk API, and market data integrations are tested.

## Troubleshooting

If the bot exits on boot, check TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN.

If wallet create/import is disabled, set WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET.

If /balance says unavailable, set RPC_URL.

If quotes are unavailable, set DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL.

If safety checks say unavailable, configure MARKET_DATA_API_URL and RISK_API_URL.

Bot: Production-ready Telegram Trading and Sniper Bot Plan

Summary:
Build a fast Telegram bot that lets users manage wallets, buy and sell tokens, configure snipes, track positions, and receive safety warnings before risky actions.

The bot should be designed as a single Node.js service using grammY for Telegram interactions, MongoDB for durable state, and a chain adapter layer for wallet, pricing, liquidity, and transaction execution. The product should prioritize short replies, inline buttons, clear confirmations, strong private-key handling, and safe defaults.

Product goals:
1) Give users a simple trading interface inside Telegram.

Users should be able to create, import, or connect a wallet, then trade with commands such as /buy, /sell, /snipe, /balance, and /positions. The bot should avoid long forms and instead use short prompts, inline buttons, and reusable presets.

2) Make sniping configurable but not overwhelming.

Snipe settings should include trade amount, slippage, max buy, gas or priority fee where supported, liquidity threshold, start condition, and optional auto-sell rules such as take-profit and stop-loss. Users should be able to save defaults globally and override them for a specific token.

3) Track positions clearly.

For every token position, the bot should show size, average entry price, current estimated value, realized PnL, unrealized PnL, total cost, and relevant transaction history. PnL should be presented as an estimate when pricing data is incomplete or liquidity is thin.

4) Protect users from common mistakes.

The bot should warn about low liquidity, suspicious token properties, high slippage, unusually large trades, failed simulation, excessive exposure, and transactions above the user’s configured max percentage per trade. Big buys should require explicit confirmation.

5) Keep actions fast.

Common actions should fit into one or two taps after initial setup. The bot should cache non-sensitive market data briefly, keep user settings ready in memory after loading from MongoDB, and use short status updates such as preparing, submitted, confirmed, or failed.

High-level architecture:
1) Single service structure.

Run one Node.js ESM process that owns the Telegram bot, user session handling, trading orchestration, wallet operations, MongoDB access, and in-process background tasks. The service starts grammY using TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables and initializes MongoDB plus chain adapters on boot.

2) Main modules.

Telegram interface: grammY command handlers, callback query handlers, conversations or stateful flows, error boundaries, rate limits, and compact message formatting.

User and settings service: loads and saves user profiles, wallet metadata, trading defaults, snipe presets, safety limits, and notification preferences.

Wallet service: supports wallet creation, import, and external connection metadata. For created or imported wallets, private keys must be encrypted before persistence. The bot should never display a private key after setup except through a deliberate export flow with repeated confirmation.

Trading service: validates inputs, computes trade size, checks safety rules, estimates output, builds transactions, requests confirmation when needed, submits transactions, tracks status, and updates positions.

Snipe service: maintains active snipe rules in MongoDB and an in-memory runtime registry. It polls or subscribes through supported chain data sources where available, evaluates trigger conditions, performs safety checks, and executes configured buys. Since the service is a single process, in-process scheduling is acceptable, with MongoDB used as the source of truth for recovery after restart.

Position service: reconciles buys, sells, fees, token balances, and price estimates into position records. It should update immediately after bot-initiated trades and periodically reconcile against on-chain balances.

Risk engine: evaluates max percentage per trade, liquidity, slippage, token age if available, ownership or authority flags where supported, transfer restrictions if detectable, tax or fee behavior where detectable, and whether the trade simulation looks abnormal.

Market data and chain adapter layer: abstracts the target blockchain and trading venue details. It exposes methods for balances, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction submission, and confirmation tracking.

3) Interaction model.

Commands start flows, inline buttons handle quick decisions, and callback data should be compact and signed or mapped to server-side state to avoid trusting client-provided values. Messages should be edited in place for status updates when possible to reduce chat noise.

4) Reliability model.

All critical actions should be idempotent. A trade request gets an internal action id before transaction submission. If Telegram retries an update or a user taps twice, the service should detect duplicate action ids and prevent double execution. MongoDB stores transaction state transitions so the bot can resume pending confirmations after restart.

5) Security model.

Use environment variables for secrets, encrypt sensitive wallet material, separate display data from secret data, require confirmation for exports and large trades, and redact secrets from logs. Admin-only diagnostics should be gated by Telegram user id allowlists stored in configuration or MongoDB.

Data model:
1) User.

Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, createdAt, lastSeenAt, status, defaultWalletId, riskProfile, globalTradingSettings, notificationSettings, role, and feature flags.

2) Wallet.

Fields: walletId, telegramUserId, chain, type, publicAddress, encryptedSecret if custodial or imported, connectionMetadata if externally connected, label, createdAt, lastUsedAt, archivedAt, and exportLockedUntil if needed.

3) Trading settings.

Fields: telegramUserId, defaultAmount, defaultSlippageBps, maxBuyAmount, maxPercentPerTrade, gasOrPriorityFeePreset, customFeeValue, requireConfirmationAboveAmount, autoSellDefaults, mevOrprivacyPreference if applicable to the chain, and updatedAt.

4) Snipe order.

Fields: snipeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol if known, status, amount, slippageBps, maxBuyAmount, minimumLiquidity, gasOrPriorityFee, triggerType, triggerParams, autoSellTakeProfitPercent, autoSellStopLossPercent, expiresAt, createdAt, updatedAt, executedTradeId, failureReason, and retryPolicy.

5) Trade.

Fields: tradeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, side, tokenAddress, baseAsset, requestedAmount, estimatedOutput, actualInput, actualOutput, slippageBps, feeEstimate, transactionHash, status, riskSnapshot, quoteSnapshot, confirmationRequired, confirmationStatus, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt, submittedAt, confirmedAt, and finalizedAt.

6) Position.

Fields: positionId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol, tokenDecimals, status, size, averageEntryPrice, totalCost, realizedPnl, unrealizedPnlEstimate, currentPriceEstimate, currentValueEstimate, feesPaidEstimate, openedAt, updatedAt, and closedAt.

7) Token risk snapshot.

Fields: chain, tokenAddress, checkedAt, liquidityEstimate, holderOrdistributionSignals if available, ownershipOrauthoritySignals if available, transferRestrictionSignals if available, simulationResult, warnings, severity, and dataQuality.

8) Session state.

Use grammY session storage backed by MongoDB for durable multi-step flows. Short-lived non-critical state can be held in memory, but anything related to pending trades, confirmations, wallet setup, or active snipes should be persisted.

9) Audit log.

Store user-visible security and trading events: wallet created, wallet imported, export requested, settings changed, snipe created, snipe cancelled, trade confirmed, trade submitted, trade failed, and admin action. Do not store raw secrets in audit records.

Key flows:
1) Onboarding and wallet setup.

User sends /start. The bot explains the core actions and asks the user to create, import, or connect a wallet. Create generates a wallet, stores encrypted secret material, shows the public address, and tells the user to back up through a secure export flow. Import asks for the private key or seed only inside a strict flow, validates it, encrypts it, and deletes sensitive prompt messages when possible. Connect stores external wallet metadata and explains which actions may require external approval.

2) Buy flow.

User sends /buy token amount or taps Buy from a token card. The bot resolves token metadata, loads wallet and settings, fetches a quote, runs risk checks, and replies with a compact preview: token, amount in, estimated amount out, price impact, slippage, liquidity warning if any, and fee estimate. If the trade is small and within safety limits, the user can confirm with one tap or use a saved fast-buy preset. If the trade exceeds thresholds, the bot requires explicit confirmation.

3) Sell flow.

User sends /sell token percent or chooses from /positions. The bot shows current position, estimated value, PnL, price impact, and expected output. Quick buttons should include 25%, 50%, 100%, and custom. The bot runs the same quote, simulation, and risk checks before submission.

4) Snipe setup flow.

User sends /snipe token. The bot shows a settings summary with amount, slippage, max buy, fee preset, liquidity threshold, and auto-sell. The user can create immediately with defaults or edit individual fields. Once activated, the snipe appears in active snipes and can be paused or cancelled.

5) Snipe execution flow.

The snipe service monitors active rules. When a trigger is met, it revalidates wallet balance, amount limits, liquidity, quote, token risk, and fee settings. If the rule is still valid, it creates a trade record, submits the transaction, updates the user with status, and updates the related position on confirmation. If auto-sell is enabled, it creates monitoring rules for take-profit and stop-loss after the buy is confirmed.

6) Balance and positions flow.

/balance shows wallet address, base asset balance, estimated token portfolio value, and any data quality warning. /positions lists open positions with symbol, size, entry, current estimate, and PnL. Selecting a position opens actions: sell, refresh, set auto-sell, view trades, or hide dust.

7) Safety flow.

Before any risky action, the risk engine returns a severity level: info, warning, high risk, or blocked. Info and normal warnings can be acknowledged with a tap. High-risk trades require an explicit confirmation phrase or a second confirmation step. Blocked trades should explain the reason and show settings that can be adjusted only if it is safe to allow override.

8) Recovery flow.

On startup, the service loads pending trades and active snipes from MongoDB. It checks any transaction that was submitted but not finalized, reconciles positions, and rebuilds the in-memory snipe registry. Users should not need to recreate snipes after a restart.

Tech stack:
1) Runtime and language.

Use a single Node.js service with ESM modules. The Telegram bot uses grammY and reads the bot token from TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN in environment variables.

2) Persistence.

Use MongoDB for users, wallets, settings, snipes, trades, positions, sessions, and audit logs. In-memory maps may be used only for short-lived caches, callback correlation, rate limiting, and active runtime registries that can be rebuilt from MongoDB.

3) Telegram framework.

Use grammY middleware for sessions, command routing, callback queries, conversations or structured multi-step flows, error handling, and rate limiting. Keep handlers thin and move business logic into services.

4) Blockchain integration.

Create a chain adapter interface for wallet derivation or validation, balance reads, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction building, submission, and confirmation tracking. This keeps the bot adaptable if the target chain or venue changes.

5) Storage for files.

If the bot later needs generated reports, exported CSV files, or chart images, store them in object storage or simple filesystem storage. Do not store wallet secrets in files.

6) Deployment.

Deploy as a generic Node.js server in the cloud. Use environment variables for configuration, a managed process lifecycle, health checks, structured logs, and regular MongoDB backups. No additional databases, message queues, or external infrastructure are required for the core design.

Non-functional requirements:
1) Security.

Encrypt private wallet material before storing it. Keep encryption keys outside MongoDB in environment-managed secrets. Never log private keys, seed phrases, raw signed transactions if sensitive, or full user-provided secrets. Add confirmation gates for wallet export, big trades, and dangerous settings.

2) Performance.

Most command responses should acknowledge within one second, even if execution continues asynchronously. Use short-lived caches for token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, and user settings. Edit existing Telegram messages for progress updates instead of sending many new messages.

3) Reliability.

Persist every trade before submission. Use clear transaction states: created, awaiting confirmation, submitted, confirmed, failed, expired, and reconciled. Make callback actions idempotent so repeated taps cannot execute duplicate trades.

4) Observability.

Use structured logs with request ids, telegram user ids, action ids, trade ids, and transaction hashes. Track error rates, failed quotes, failed submissions, slow chain calls, and snipe execution outcomes. Provide an admin-only status command for service health and pending operations.

5) Compliance and user communication.

Show clear risk disclaimers during onboarding and before high-risk trading. Make it obvious that PnL and price data are estimates. Provide commands to export basic user data, delete bot data where feasible, and revoke or archive wallets from the bot interface.

6) Abuse prevention.

Apply per-user rate limits, block repeated invalid token lookups, limit the number of active snipes per user by plan or configuration, and protect admin commands with an allowlist. Validate all Telegram callback data against server-side state.

7) Maintainability.

Keep Telegram handlers separate from trading logic, wallet logic, risk logic, and persistence. Use typed configuration, consistent error codes, integration tests for critical flows, and test wallets on non-production environments before enabling real trading.

Bot commands:
• start — Starts onboarding, explains the bot, and shows the main menu with wallet, trading, positions, and settings actions. (usage: /start) [core]
• wallet — Shows the active wallet, public address, wallet status, and actions to create, import, connect, export, switch, or archive a wallet. (usage: /wallet) [wallet]
• buy — Starts a token buy flow with quote preview, safety checks, and confirmation buttons. (usage: /buy <tokenaddress> <amount>) [trading]
• sell — Starts a token sell flow. Supports exact amount, percentage, or quick selection from current positions. (usage: /sell <tokenaddress> <percentoramount>) [trading]
• snipe — Creates or manages a snipe order using saved defaults, editable amount, slippage, max buy, fee, liquidity threshold, and optional auto-sell. (usage: /snipe <tokenaddress>) [sniping]
• snipes — Lists active, paused, executed, and failed snipes with actions to edit, pause, resume, or cancel. (usage: /snipes) [sniping]
• balance — Shows wallet balance, estimated portfolio value, and recent refresh status. (usage: /balance) [portfolio]
• positions — Lists open token positions with size, average entry, current estimate, and PnL. Each position opens sell, refresh, and auto-sell actions. (usage: /positions) [portfolio]
• settings — Opens trading defaults such as amount, slippage, max percent per trade, max buy, fee preset, confirmation threshold, and auto-sell defaults. (usage: /settings) [settings]
• risk — Shows or edits safety settings and can run a token risk check without trading. (usage: /risk [tokenaddress]) [safety]
• history — Shows recent trades, transaction statuses, realized PnL, and failed actions. (usage: /history) [portfolio]
• help — Shows a short command reference and recommended first steps. (usage: /help) [core]

planSections.productGoals:
1) Give users a simple trading interface inside Telegram.

Users should be able to create, import, or connect a wallet, then trade with commands such as /buy, /sell, /snipe, /balance, and /positions. The bot should avoid long forms and instead use short prompts, inline buttons, and reusable presets.

2) Make sniping configurable but not overwhelming.

Snipe settings should include trade amount, slippage, max buy, gas or priority fee where supported, liquidity threshold, start condition, and optional auto-sell rules such as take-profit and stop-loss. Users should be able to save defaults globally and override them for a specific token.

3) Track positions clearly.

For every token position, the bot should show size, average entry price, current estimated value, realized PnL, unrealized PnL, total cost, and relevant transaction history. PnL should be presented as an estimate when pricing data is incomplete or liquidity is thin.

4) Protect users from common mistakes.

The bot should warn about low liquidity, suspicious token properties, high slippage, unusually large trades, failed simulation, excessive exposure, and transactions above the user’s configured max percentage per trade. Big buys should require explicit confirmation.

5) Keep actions fast.

Common actions should fit into one or two taps after initial setup. The bot should cache non-sensitive market data briefly, keep user settings ready in memory after loading from MongoDB, and use short status updates such as preparing, submitted, confirmed, or failed.
planSections.highLevelArchitecture:
1) Single service structure.

Run one Node.js ESM process that owns the Telegram bot, user session handling, trading orchestration, wallet operations, MongoDB access, and in-process background tasks. The service starts grammY using TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables and initializes MongoDB plus chain adapters on boot.

2) Main modules.

Telegram interface: grammY command handlers, callback query handlers, conversations or stateful flows, error boundaries, rate limits, and compact message formatting.

User and settings service: loads and saves user profiles, wallet metadata, trading defaults, snipe presets, safety limits, and notification preferences.

Wallet service: supports wallet creation, import, and external connection metadata. For created or imported wallets, private keys must be encrypted before persistence. The bot should never display a private key after setup except through a deliberate export flow with repeated confirmation.

Trading service: validates inputs, computes trade size, checks safety rules, estimates output, builds transactions, requests confirmation when needed, submits transactions, tracks status, and updates positions.

Snipe service: maintains active snipe rules in MongoDB and an in-memory runtime registry. It polls or subscribes through supported chain data sources where available, evaluates trigger conditions, performs safety checks, and executes configured buys. Since the service is a single process, in-process scheduling is acceptable, with MongoDB used as the source of truth for recovery after restart.

Position service: reconciles buys, sells, fees, token balances, and price estimates into position records. It should update immediately after bot-initiated trades and periodically reconcile against on-chain balances.

Risk engine: evaluates max percentage per trade, liquidity, slippage, token age if available, ownership or authority flags where supported, transfer restrictions if detectable, tax or fee behavior where detectable, and whether the trade simulation looks abnormal.

Market data and chain adapter layer: abstracts the target blockchain and trading venue details. It exposes methods for balances, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction submission, and confirmation tracking.

3) Interaction model.

Commands start flows, inline buttons handle quick decisions, and callback data should be compact and signed or mapped to server-side state to avoid trusting client-provided values. Messages should be edited in place for status updates when possible to reduce chat noise.

4) Reliability model.

All critical actions should be idempotent. A trade request gets an internal action id before transaction submission. If Telegram retries an update or a user taps twice, the service should detect duplicate action ids and prevent double execution. MongoDB stores transaction state transitions so the bot can resume pending confirmations after restart.

5) Security model.

Use environment variables for secrets, encrypt sensitive wallet material, separate display data from secret data, require confirmation for exports and large trades, and redact secrets from logs. Admin-only diagnostics should be gated by Telegram user id allowlists stored in configuration or MongoDB.

planSections.keyFlows:
1) Onboarding and wallet setup.

User sends /start. The bot explains the core actions and asks the user to create, import, or connect a wallet. Create generates a wallet, stores encrypted secret material, shows the public address, and tells the user to back up through a secure export flow. Import asks for the private key or seed only inside a strict flow, validates it, encrypts it, and deletes sensitive prompt messages when possible. Connect stores external wallet metadata and explains which actions may require external approval.

2) Buy flow.

User sends /buy token amount or taps Buy from a token card. The bot resolves token metadata, loads wallet and settings, fetches a quote, runs risk checks, and replies with a compact preview: token, amount in, estimated amount out, price impact, slippage, liquidity warning if any, and fee estimate. If the trade is small and within safety limits, the user can confirm with one tap or use a saved fast-buy preset. If the trade exceeds thresholds, the bot requires explicit confirmation.

3) Sell flow.

User sends /sell token percent or chooses from /positions. The bot shows current position, estimated value, PnL, price impact, and expected output. Quick buttons should include 25%, 50%, 100%, and custom. The bot runs the same quote, simulation, and risk checks before submission.

4) Snipe setup flow.

User sends /snipe token. The bot shows a settings summary with amount, slippage, max buy, fee preset, liquidity threshold, and auto-sell. The user can create immediately with defaults or edit individual fields. Once activated, the snipe appears in active snipes and can be paused or cancelled.

5) Snipe execution flow.

The snipe service monitors active rules. When a trigger is met, it revalidates wallet balance, amount limits, liquidity, quote, token risk, and fee settings. If the rule is still valid, it creates a trade record, submits the transaction, updates the user with status, and updates the related position on confirmation. If auto-sell is enabled, it creates monitoring rules for take-profit and stop-loss after the buy is confirmed.

6) Balance and positions flow.

/balance shows wallet address, base asset balance, estimated token portfolio value, and any data quality warning. /positions lists open positions with symbol, size, entry, current estimate, and PnL. Selecting a position opens actions: sell, refresh, set auto-sell, view trades, or hide dust.

7) Safety flow.

Before any risky action, the risk engine returns a severity level: info, warning, high risk, or blocked. Info and normal warnings can be acknowledged with a tap. High-risk trades require an explicit confirmation phrase or a second confirmation step. Blocked trades should explain the reason and show settings that can be adjusted only if it is safe to allow override.

8) Recovery flow.

On startup, the service loads pending trades and active snipes from MongoDB. It checks any transaction that was submitted but not finalized, reconciles positions, and rebuilds the in-memory snipe registry. Users should not need to recreate snipes after a restart.
planSections.techStack:
1) Runtime and language.

Use a single Node.js service with ESM modules. The Telegram bot uses grammY and reads the bot token from TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN in environment variables.

2) Persistence.

Use MongoDB for users, wallets, settings, snipes, trades, positions, sessions, and audit logs. In-memory maps may be used only for short-lived caches, callback correlation, rate limiting, and active runtime registries that can be rebuilt from MongoDB.

3) Telegram framework.

Use grammY middleware for sessions, command routing, callback queries, conversations or structured multi-step flows, error handling, and rate limiting. Keep handlers thin and move business logic into services.

4) Blockchain integration.

Create a chain adapter interface for wallet derivation or validation, balance reads, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction building, submission, and confirmation tracking. This keeps the bot adaptable if the target chain or venue changes.

5) Storage for files.

If the bot later needs generated reports, exported CSV files, or chart images, store them in object storage or simple filesystem storage. Do not store wallet secrets in files.

6) Deployment.

Deploy as a generic Node.js server in the cloud. Use environment variables for configuration, a managed process lifecycle, health checks, structured logs, and regular MongoDB backups. No additional databases, message queues, or external infrastructure are required for the core design.
planSections.nonFunctional:
1) Security.

Encrypt private wallet material before storing it. Keep encryption keys outside MongoDB in environment-managed secrets. Never log private keys, seed phrases, raw signed transactions if sensitive, or full user-provided secrets. Add confirmation gates for wallet export, big trades, and dangerous settings.

2) Performance.

Most command responses should acknowledge within one second, even if execution continues asynchronously. Use short-lived caches for token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, and user settings. Edit existing Telegram messages for progress updates instead of sending many new messages.

3) Reliability.

Persist every trade before submission. Use clear transaction states: created, awaiting confirmation, submitted, confirmed, failed, expired, and reconciled. Make callback actions idempotent so repeated taps cannot execute duplicate trades.

4) Observability.

Use structured logs with request ids, telegram user ids, action ids, trade ids, and transaction hashes. Track error rates, failed quotes, failed submissions, slow chain calls, and snipe execution outcomes. Provide an admin-only status command for service health and pending operations.

5) Compliance and user communication.

Show clear risk disclaimers during onboarding and before high-risk trading. Make it obvious that PnL and price data are estimates. Provide commands to export basic user data, delete bot data where feasible, and revoke or archive wallets from the bot interface.

6) Abuse prevention.

Apply per-user rate limits, block repeated invalid token lookups, limit the number of active snipes per user by plan or configuration, and protect admin commands with an allowlist. Validate all Telegram callback data against server-side state.

7) Maintainability.

Keep Telegram handlers separate from trading logic, wallet logic, risk logic, and persistence. Use typed configuration, consistent error codes, integration tests for critical flows, and test wallets on non-production environments before enabling real trading.

DOCS.md.content:
# Trading Sniper Bot

This is a Telegram-only trading and sniping bot built with Node.js ES modules and grammY.

It helps users create or import an encrypted wallet, preview buys and sells, configure snipe targets, track positions, and edit trading safety settings.

Crypto trading and sniping are high risk. This bot is not financial advice.

## Commands

/start
Opens the main menu and shows the risk disclaimer.

/help
Shows commands, wallet requirements, safety checks, and the recommended flow.

/wallet
Create a new wallet, import a wallet, view the active public address, or delete stored wallet data.

/buy <tokenAddress> <amount> [slippage]
Starts a buy preview. The bot fetches a quote when a DEX aggregator is configured, checks risk and liquidity when configured, then requires confirmation.

/sell <tokenAddress> <amountOrPercent> [slippage]
Starts a sell preview. You can also select a position and use 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% buttons.

/snipe [tokenAddress]
Creates a guided snipe target using your defaults for amount, slippage, max buy, priority fee, take-profit, and stop-loss.

/balance
Shows native balance and tracked token positions. Requires a wallet and RPC_URL.

/positions
Shows open positions with size, average entry, and basic estimated PnL status.

/settings
Opens inline buttons to edit default amount, slippage, max buy, max percent per trade, priority fee, take-profit, stop-loss, and confirmation preferences.

## Environment variables

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required for Telegram.

MONGODB_URI enables persistent storage for users, wallets, snipes, trades, and positions. If missing, the bot starts with limited in-memory fallback.

WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET is required for wallet creation and import. Wallet secrets are encrypted at rest. Private keys and seed phrases are never logged or echoed.

RPC_URL is used for native balance checks.

CHAIN_ID defaults to 1.

NATIVE_SYMBOL defaults to ETH.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL enables quote and execution provider calls.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_API_KEY is optional and sent only to the configured aggregator.

MARKET_DATA_API_URL enables liquidity checks.

RISK_API_URL enables risky-token scoring.

TRADING_ENABLED defaults to false. When false, the bot runs quote and preview flows only.

SNIPE_POLL_INTERVAL_MS defaults to 15000.

## Safety behavior

The bot validates token addresses before trading.

It warns when quotes are unavailable, liquidity checks are unavailable, risk scoring is unavailable, liquidity appears low, the risk API reports danger, or the trade exceeds max buy settings.

All transactions require explicit confirmation. Preview mode is used when TRADING_ENABLED=false.

## MongoDB collections

users stores Telegram metadata and trading settings.

wallets stores public wallet data and encrypted secret payloads.

snipes stores active and historical snipe targets.

trades stores quote, status, transaction hash, and failure summaries.

positions stores tracked token positions and average entry data.

createdAt is insert-only. Updates use updatedAt.

## Deployment

Install dependencies with npm run build.

Start with npm start.

On Render, set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and MONGODB_URI. Add WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET before enabling wallet creation or import. Keep TRADING_ENABLED=false until provider integrations are tested.

The bot runs as one Node.js process. The snipe poller runs inside the same process.

README.md.content:
# Trading Sniper Bot

Telegram-only trading/sniping bot using Node.js ES modules, grammY, MongoDB, encrypted wallet storage, inline menus, preview-first trading, and a single-process snipe polling loop.

## Features

1) Wallet creation, import, view, and delete.
2) Encrypted wallet secrets using WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET.
3) Buy and sell preview flows with confirmation.
4) Snipe target storage and polling.
5) Balance and position views.
6) Editable trading settings.
7) Liquidity and risk warnings when APIs are configured.
8) Preview-only mode unless TRADING_ENABLED=true.

## Setup

1) Install dependencies.

npm run build

2) Copy .env.sample to .env and fill values.

3) Start locally.

npm run dev

4) Start production.

npm start

## Required env

TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN is required.

MONGODB_URI is strongly recommended for persistence.

WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET is required before wallet creation or import works.

## Optional env

RPC_URL enables /balance.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL enables /buy and /sell quotes and execution provider calls.

DEX_AGGREGATOR_API_KEY is optional provider auth.

MARKET_DATA_API_URL enables liquidity checks.

RISK_API_URL enables token risk scoring.

TRADING_ENABLED defaults to false.

## Commands

/start opens the main menu.

/help shows usage and safety notes.

/wallet opens wallet setup.

/buy <tokenAddress> <amount> [slippage] previews a buy.

/sell <tokenAddress> <amountOrPercent> [slippage] previews a sell.

/snipe [tokenAddress] creates a snipe target.

/balance shows native balance and tracked positions.

/positions lists open positions.

/settings edits defaults and safety limits.

## Architecture

src/index.js boots the app, validates Telegram config, connects MongoDB, starts the bot, and starts the in-process snipe poller.

src/bot.js creates the grammY bot and registers command modules before catch-all flow handlers.

src/commands contains public command modules.

src/features/tradingUi.js owns inline menus, callbacks, and multi-step flows.

src/services contains wallet, user, market, trading, position, and snipe logic.

src/lib contains config, logging, database, crypto, and UI helpers.

## Database

Collections: users, wallets, snipes, trades, positions.

Indexes are created only for application fields, never _id.

Upserts keep createdAt in $setOnInsert and updatedAt in $set.

## Deployment notes

Use one Node.js service. Do not run a separate worker.

The bot clears Telegram webhooks before long polling.

The snipe poller logs start, cycles, failures, and memory usage.

Keep TRADING_ENABLED=false until your RPC, aggregator, risk API, and market data integrations are tested.

## Troubleshooting

If the bot exits on boot, check TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN.

If wallet create/import is disabled, set WALLET_ENCRYPTION_SECRET.

If /balance says unavailable, set RPC_URL.

If quotes are unavailable, set DEX_AGGREGATOR_BASE_URL.

If safety checks say unavailable, configure MARKET_DATA_API_URL and RISK_API_URL.

Product goals:
1) Give users a simple trading interface inside Telegram.

Users should be able to create, import, or connect a wallet, then trade with commands such as /buy, /sell, /snipe, /balance, and /positions. The bot should avoid long forms and instead use short prompts, inline buttons, and reusable presets.

2) Make sniping configurable but not overwhelming.

Snipe settings should include trade amount, slippage, max buy, gas or priority fee where supported, liquidity threshold, start condition, and optional auto-sell rules such as take-profit and stop-loss. Users should be able to save defaults globally and override them for a specific token.

3) Track positions clearly.

For every token position, the bot should show size, average entry price, current estimated value, realized PnL, unrealized PnL, total cost, and relevant transaction history. PnL should be presented as an estimate when pricing data is incomplete or liquidity is thin.

4) Protect users from common mistakes.

The bot should warn about low liquidity, suspicious token properties, high slippage, unusually large trades, failed simulation, excessive exposure, and transactions above the user’s configured max percentage per trade. Big buys should require explicit confirmation.

5) Keep actions fast.

Common actions should fit into one or two taps after initial setup. The bot should cache non-sensitive market data briefly, keep user settings ready in memory after loading from MongoDB, and use short status updates such as preparing, submitted, confirmed, or failed.

High-level architecture:
1) Single service structure.

Run one Node.js ESM process that owns the Telegram bot, user session handling, trading orchestration, wallet operations, MongoDB access, and in-process background tasks. The service starts grammY using TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables and initializes MongoDB plus chain adapters on boot.

2) Main modules.

Telegram interface: grammY command handlers, callback query handlers, conversations or stateful flows, error boundaries, rate limits, and compact message formatting.

User and settings service: loads and saves user profiles, wallet metadata, trading defaults, snipe presets, safety limits, and notification preferences.

Wallet service: supports wallet creation, import, and external connection metadata. For created or imported wallets, private keys must be encrypted before persistence. The bot should never display a private key after setup except through a deliberate export flow with repeated confirmation.

Trading service: validates inputs, computes trade size, checks safety rules, estimates output, builds transactions, requests confirmation when needed, submits transactions, tracks status, and updates positions.

Snipe service: maintains active snipe rules in MongoDB and an in-memory runtime registry. It polls or subscribes through supported chain data sources where available, evaluates trigger conditions, performs safety checks, and executes configured buys. Since the service is a single process, in-process scheduling is acceptable, with MongoDB used as the source of truth for recovery after restart.

Position service: reconciles buys, sells, fees, token balances, and price estimates into position records. It should update immediately after bot-initiated trades and periodically reconcile against on-chain balances.

Risk engine: evaluates max percentage per trade, liquidity, slippage, token age if available, ownership or authority flags where supported, transfer restrictions if detectable, tax or fee behavior where detectable, and whether the trade simulation looks abnormal.

Market data and chain adapter layer: abstracts the target blockchain and trading venue details. It exposes methods for balances, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction submission, and confirmation tracking.

3) Interaction model.

Commands start flows, inline buttons handle quick decisions, and callback data should be compact and signed or mapped to server-side state to avoid trusting client-provided values. Messages should be edited in place for status updates when possible to reduce chat noise.

4) Reliability model.

All critical actions should be idempotent. A trade request gets an internal action id before transaction submission. If Telegram retries an update or a user taps twice, the service should detect duplicate action ids and prevent double execution. MongoDB stores transaction state transitions so the bot can resume pending confirmations after restart.

5) Security model.

Use environment variables for secrets, encrypt sensitive wallet material, separate display data from secret data, require confirmation for exports and large trades, and redact secrets from logs. Admin-only diagnostics should be gated by Telegram user id allowlists stored in configuration or MongoDB.

Data model:
1) User.

Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, createdAt, lastSeenAt, status, defaultWalletId, riskProfile, globalTradingSettings, notificationSettings, role, and feature flags.

2) Wallet.

Fields: walletId, telegramUserId, chain, type, publicAddress, encryptedSecret if custodial or imported, connectionMetadata if externally connected, label, createdAt, lastUsedAt, archivedAt, and exportLockedUntil if needed.

3) Trading settings.

Fields: telegramUserId, defaultAmount, defaultSlippageBps, maxBuyAmount, maxPercentPerTrade, gasOrPriorityFeePreset, customFeeValue, requireConfirmationAboveAmount, autoSellDefaults, mevOrprivacyPreference if applicable to the chain, and updatedAt.

4) Snipe order.

Fields: snipeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol if known, status, amount, slippageBps, maxBuyAmount, minimumLiquidity, gasOrPriorityFee, triggerType, triggerParams, autoSellTakeProfitPercent, autoSellStopLossPercent, expiresAt, createdAt, updatedAt, executedTradeId, failureReason, and retryPolicy.

5) Trade.

Fields: tradeId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, side, tokenAddress, baseAsset, requestedAmount, estimatedOutput, actualInput, actualOutput, slippageBps, feeEstimate, transactionHash, status, riskSnapshot, quoteSnapshot, confirmationRequired, confirmationStatus, errorCode, errorMessage, createdAt, submittedAt, confirmedAt, and finalizedAt.

6) Position.

Fields: positionId, telegramUserId, walletId, chain, tokenAddress, tokenSymbol, tokenDecimals, status, size, averageEntryPrice, totalCost, realizedPnl, unrealizedPnlEstimate, currentPriceEstimate, currentValueEstimate, feesPaidEstimate, openedAt, updatedAt, and closedAt.

7) Token risk snapshot.

Fields: chain, tokenAddress, checkedAt, liquidityEstimate, holderOrdistributionSignals if available, ownershipOrauthoritySignals if available, transferRestrictionSignals if available, simulationResult, warnings, severity, and dataQuality.

8) Session state.

Use grammY session storage backed by MongoDB for durable multi-step flows. Short-lived non-critical state can be held in memory, but anything related to pending trades, confirmations, wallet setup, or active snipes should be persisted.

9) Audit log.

Store user-visible security and trading events: wallet created, wallet imported, export requested, settings changed, snipe created, snipe cancelled, trade confirmed, trade submitted, trade failed, and admin action. Do not store raw secrets in audit records.

Key flows:
1) Onboarding and wallet setup.

User sends /start. The bot explains the core actions and asks the user to create, import, or connect a wallet. Create generates a wallet, stores encrypted secret material, shows the public address, and tells the user to back up through a secure export flow. Import asks for the private key or seed only inside a strict flow, validates it, encrypts it, and deletes sensitive prompt messages when possible. Connect stores external wallet metadata and explains which actions may require external approval.

2) Buy flow.

User sends /buy token amount or taps Buy from a token card. The bot resolves token metadata, loads wallet and settings, fetches a quote, runs risk checks, and replies with a compact preview: token, amount in, estimated amount out, price impact, slippage, liquidity warning if any, and fee estimate. If the trade is small and within safety limits, the user can confirm with one tap or use a saved fast-buy preset. If the trade exceeds thresholds, the bot requires explicit confirmation.

3) Sell flow.

User sends /sell token percent or chooses from /positions. The bot shows current position, estimated value, PnL, price impact, and expected output. Quick buttons should include 25%, 50%, 100%, and custom. The bot runs the same quote, simulation, and risk checks before submission.

4) Snipe setup flow.

User sends /snipe token. The bot shows a settings summary with amount, slippage, max buy, fee preset, liquidity threshold, and auto-sell. The user can create immediately with defaults or edit individual fields. Once activated, the snipe appears in active snipes and can be paused or cancelled.

5) Snipe execution flow.

The snipe service monitors active rules. When a trigger is met, it revalidates wallet balance, amount limits, liquidity, quote, token risk, and fee settings. If the rule is still valid, it creates a trade record, submits the transaction, updates the user with status, and updates the related position on confirmation. If auto-sell is enabled, it creates monitoring rules for take-profit and stop-loss after the buy is confirmed.

6) Balance and positions flow.

/balance shows wallet address, base asset balance, estimated token portfolio value, and any data quality warning. /positions lists open positions with symbol, size, entry, current estimate, and PnL. Selecting a position opens actions: sell, refresh, set auto-sell, view trades, or hide dust.

7) Safety flow.

Before any risky action, the risk engine returns a severity level: info, warning, high risk, or blocked. Info and normal warnings can be acknowledged with a tap. High-risk trades require an explicit confirmation phrase or a second confirmation step. Blocked trades should explain the reason and show settings that can be adjusted only if it is safe to allow override.

8) Recovery flow.

On startup, the service loads pending trades and active snipes from MongoDB. It checks any transaction that was submitted but not finalized, reconciles positions, and rebuilds the in-memory snipe registry. Users should not need to recreate snipes after a restart.

Tech stack:
1) Runtime and language.

Use a single Node.js service with ESM modules. The Telegram bot uses grammY and reads the bot token from TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN in environment variables.

2) Persistence.

Use MongoDB for users, wallets, settings, snipes, trades, positions, sessions, and audit logs. In-memory maps may be used only for short-lived caches, callback correlation, rate limiting, and active runtime registries that can be rebuilt from MongoDB.

3) Telegram framework.

Use grammY middleware for sessions, command routing, callback queries, conversations or structured multi-step flows, error handling, and rate limiting. Keep handlers thin and move business logic into services.

4) Blockchain integration.

Create a chain adapter interface for wallet derivation or validation, balance reads, token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, transaction simulation, transaction building, submission, and confirmation tracking. This keeps the bot adaptable if the target chain or venue changes.

5) Storage for files.

If the bot later needs generated reports, exported CSV files, or chart images, store them in object storage or simple filesystem storage. Do not store wallet secrets in files.

6) Deployment.

Deploy as a generic Node.js server in the cloud. Use environment variables for configuration, a managed process lifecycle, health checks, structured logs, and regular MongoDB backups. No additional databases, message queues, or external infrastructure are required for the core design.

Non-functional requirements:
1) Security.

Encrypt private wallet material before storing it. Keep encryption keys outside MongoDB in environment-managed secrets. Never log private keys, seed phrases, raw signed transactions if sensitive, or full user-provided secrets. Add confirmation gates for wallet export, big trades, and dangerous settings.

2) Performance.

Most command responses should acknowledge within one second, even if execution continues asynchronously. Use short-lived caches for token metadata, quotes, liquidity checks, and user settings. Edit existing Telegram messages for progress updates instead of sending many new messages.

3) Reliability.

Persist every trade before submission. Use clear transaction states: created, awaiting confirmation, submitted, confirmed, failed, expired, and reconciled. Make callback actions idempotent so repeated taps cannot execute duplicate trades.

4) Observability.

Use structured logs with request ids, telegram user ids, action ids, trade ids, and transaction hashes. Track error rates, failed quotes, failed submissions, slow chain calls, and snipe execution outcomes. Provide an admin-only status command for service health and pending operations.

5) Compliance and user communication.

Show clear risk disclaimers during onboarding and before high-risk trading. Make it obvious that PnL and price data are estimates. Provide commands to export basic user data, delete bot data where feasible, and revoke or archive wallets from the bot interface.

6) Abuse prevention.

Apply per-user rate limits, block repeated invalid token lookups, limit the number of active snipes per user by plan or configuration, and protect admin commands with an allowlist. Validate all Telegram callback data against server-side state.

7) Maintainability.

Keep Telegram handlers separate from trading logic, wallet logic, risk logic, and persistence. Use typed configuration, consistent error codes, integration tests for critical flows, and test wallets on non-production environments before enabling real trading.

Bot commands:
• start — Starts onboarding, explains the bot, and shows the main menu with wallet, trading, positions, and settings actions. (usage: /start) [core]
• wallet — Shows the active wallet, public address, wallet status, and actions to create, import, connect, export, switch, or archive a wallet. (usage: /wallet) [wallet]
• buy — Starts a token buy flow with quote preview, safety checks, and confirmation buttons. (usage: /buy <tokenaddress> <amount>) [trading]
• sell — Starts a token sell flow. Supports exact amount, percentage, or quick selection from current positions. (usage: /sell <tokenaddress> <percentoramount>) [trading]
• snipe — Creates or manages a snipe order using saved defaults, editable amount, slippage, max buy, fee, liquidity threshold, and optional auto-sell. (usage: /snipe <tokenaddress>) [sniping]
• snipes — Lists active, paused, executed, and failed snipes with actions to edit, pause, resume, or cancel. (usage: /snipes) [sniping]
• balance — Shows wallet balance, estimated portfolio value, and recent refresh status. (usage: /balance) [portfolio]
• positions — Lists open token positions with size, average entry, current estimate, and PnL. Each position opens sell, refresh, and auto-sell actions. (usage: /positions) [portfolio]
• settings — Opens trading defaults such as amount, slippage, max percent per trade, max buy, fee preset, confirmation threshold, and auto-sell defaults. (usage: /settings) [settings]
• risk — Shows or edits safety settings and can run a token risk check without trading. (usage: /risk [tokenaddress]) [safety]
• history — Shows recent trades, transaction statuses, realized PnL, and failed actions. (usage: /history) [portfolio]
• help — Shows a short command reference and recommended first steps. (usage: /help) [core]
